label: Dense near-constant feature: on at every step except the <DEL> delimiter
explanation: Dense, bias-like feature, active on 81% of all steps. It is strongly suppressed at the delimiter step: it fires on only 16% of <DEL> steps, which hold 1% of activation mass. Elsewhere it is on almost everywhere: 100% at t=0, about 98% at t=1, falling to roughly 40-60% late in the original phase (orig_idx 6-8), then back to about 90% throughout the copy phase. The predicate phase != 1 gets F1 0.92 and mass recall 0.99 on dev; nearly all false positives are late original-phase or end-of-copy steps where the feature is weakly off. Magnitude is largest at original steps 1-3 (about 40% of mass is at t<=3), and the top activations come from sequences beginning with d d w. Copy-phase activations are small, roughly 0.1-0.4 of max. Activation rate depends only weakly on token identity (in_tok rates 0.87-0.96, with w, f, 0 and u slightly higher). It does not depend on out_tok, next_out, first_tok or digit count. It does not fire meaningfully on the delimiter.

issues: Systematic false-positive class the explanation misses: in the copy phase the feature is off when the input token is 'd'. (phase==2)&(in_tok==d) has precision 0.080 (about 8% active, n=90,853 dev steps). Every other copy-phase input token sits at about 0.90-0.98 (a 0.93, b 0.91, c 0.92, l 0.98, 1 0.98, 0 0.90, ...). This shows up repeatedly as unhighlighted '*d*' steps in the test-split false positives.

So the claim that it 'depends only weakly on token identity (in_tok rates 0.87-0.96)' is wrong. The aggregate in_tok table hides this because 'd' is active about 93% of the time in the original phase but about 8% in the copy phase. 'd' also shapes the top activations (sequences starting d d w), and in the late original phase the rate is higher when 'd' was seen earlier (0.83 vs 0.63 at orig_idx>=4).

The second large false-positive class is the late original phase. At orig_idx>=5 precision is only 0.60, and the rate falls steadily from 1.00 at t=0 to 0.375 at orig_idx 8. The explanation notes this but calls it 'weakly off'. This is a clear dependence on position, not scattered noise. It does not depend on in_first or on whether the previous token was a digit (both about 0.60-0.67).

Claims that check out: phase != 1 scores test F1 0.923 and mass recall 0.99. The delimiter rate is 16%, holding 1% of mass. About 45% of mass is at t<=3. Rates by t, out_tok, next_out, first_tok and n_digits match what was reported. Copy phase holds 38.5% of mass at a 0.907 rate.

Better predicate: (phase==0) | ((phase==2) & (in_tok!=tok('d'))). Test precision rises from 0.869 to 0.881 and F1 from 0.923 to 0.929. Also restricting the original phase to (orig_idx<=5 or 'd' seen) raises precision to 0.910, but F1 stays at 0.928.
